column1: # The PRODUCTION-SHAPED cluster's STOPPED consumer groups.
#   group <TAB> topic <TAB> position
# `position` is passed to `kafka-consumer-groups.sh --reset-offsets` as it stands, so it is any of
# that tool's specifications: --to-earliest, --to-latest, --to-offset N, --shift-by -N.
# Not --to-datetime. Kafka stamps every record with the moment it was produced, and this whole
# cluster is produced within a few seconds of the seed running, so every time-based reset resolves
# to offset 0. seed.sh's comment on this file's format explains it at length.
# WHY THESE ARE ALL "EMPTY", AND WHERE THE LIVE ONES ARE
# A consumer group, from the outside, is nothing but a set of committed offsets. Writing those
# offsets directly creates the group without running a consumer, which is one command instead of a
# consumer session per partition, and gives an exact lag rather than an approximate one. But a
# group has MEMBERS only while some process is holding a session open with the broker, and seed.sh
# exits — so every group in this file is reported by Kafka as `Empty`: it exists, it has committed
# offsets, nobody is reading.
# That is a real and common state — it is what a stopped service looks like — and it is half of
# what the consumer-groups screen has to distinguish. The other half is the live groups, which are
# containers running consume.sh and are listed in the Compose stack, not here:
#   search-indexer        3 members, Stable, on search.index-updates — a multi-member assignment,
#                         which is what the members table exists to draw.
#   clickstream-archiver  1 member, deliberately throttled, on clickstream.raw — its lag falls
#                         while you watch it, instead of being a number that is zero for ever.
#   fraud-scoring         2 members across two topics, restarting one member on a timer, so the
#                         group passes through PreparingRebalance every minute or so. Nobody sees
#                         a rebalancing group otherwise: a healthy group rebalances once at
#                         startup and then never again.
# THE LAGS, AND WHY THEY DIFFER
# Lag that is the same everywhere is a colour, not a signal. These five are spread across three
# orders of magnitude on purpose, so that whatever KUI does to draw "behind" — a number, a bar, a
# colour — has something to distinguish.
# BADLY BEHIND. Committed at the very beginning of a topic holding eight thousand records, so the
# lag is the whole topic. This is the group an operator is looking at when something has gone
# wrong, and the one the offset-reset wizard exists for.
analytics-rollup
# HALF BEHIND. platform.metrics holds three thousand generated records spread evenly over six
# partitions — five hundred each — so committing at offset 250 leaves this group exactly half way
# through every partition. It is the middle of the three lag sizes on this cluster: not the whole
# topic like analytics-rollup, not four records like dlq-triage.
metrics-exporter
# A LITTLE BEHIND, UNEVENLY. Offset 1 in each of twelve partitions of a topic holding sixteen
# hand-written records, so some partitions are behind by two and some by none. Small, uneven,
# per-partition lag is the case a lag table gets wrong if it only ever shows a topic-level total.
order-fulfilment
# BEHIND ON THE THING THAT MATTERS MOST. Four dead letters nobody has looked at. The number is
# tiny and it is the most important number on the screen, which is the point: lag is not
# interesting in proportion to its size.
dlq-triage
# CAUGHT UP. Committed at the end of every partition, so its lag is zero. Without a group like
# this, "lag" looks like something every group has rather than a state one group is in.
payments-ledger-sync
# A group subscribed to TWO topics, caught up on one and behind on the other. A group's lag is not
# one number, and a screen that adds them together loses the only fact worth knowing.
billing-reconciler
billing-reconciler
